subject: astronomy
title: Gravity & Orbits: Foundations
welcome_lead: Gravity is the glue of the universe — it holds galaxies together.
meta_desc: KS3 astronomy: gravity, mass, weight, why planets orbit.
final_note: Drop an apple or hold up the Moon — same force.

concepts.def: Pull between any two objects with mass.
Amount of matter in an object (kg).

Moving with only gravity acting on you.

walkthroughs.body_html: Gravity pulls any two masses together. Bigger mass = stronger pull. That's why we don't notice each other's gravity but Earth's is huge.
Mass stays the same anywhere. Weight depends on local gravity. You'd weigh less on the Moon — but your mass would not change.
An astronaut in orbit is in free fall around Earth — they're falling but moving sideways fast enough to miss the ground. That's an orbit!

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an asteroid and a comet?
options: They are the same object with different names.
Asteroids are rocky/metallic; comets contain ice that vaporises near the Sun, producing a tail.
Comets are larger than asteroids.
Because clouds block them.

mcqs.q: What is the principle behind stellar parallax?
options: Because clouds block them.
A nearby star appears to shift against background stars as Earth orbits the Sun.
Telescopes distort star positions.
Stars actually move position throughout the year.

mcqs.q: Why don't we have a solar eclipse every new moon?
options: Comets are larger than asteroids.
Because clouds block them.
Eclipses happen randomly.
The Moon's orbit is tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Sun's apparent position.
